title: Raga Gujri
hookLine: a quiet morning raga, devotion that doesn't announce itself

cards: What does devotion sound like when nobody's watching? Not the big festival, not the packed hall. Something smaller.
A grandmother who covers her head and murmurs a line before she lights the stove. A man who wipes down the steps of the gurdwara before anyone arrives and leaves before anyone thanks him.
A teenager with one earbud in on the bus, listening to kirtan at low volume. None of it is loud. All of it is meant.
The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga with that temperament.

teach.b: Gujri comes after Asa in the Granth's order of ragas.

Tradition places it in the morning, and its mood is usually described as quiet and devotional: not Asa's forward lean of hope, but something more settled, like someone who has already turned toward God and simply stays turned.
Its hymns come from several of the Gurus, and from Bhagats too.

teach.h: SERVE THE LORD, AND NO OTHER.
teach.b: Here's a line from Guru Amar Das in Gujri, in plain English: serve the Lord, and serve no other. It's short, and it doesn't raise its voice. That's a fair picture of the raga.

teach.h: MUSIC FOR THE QUIET SIDE OF FAITH.
teach.b: Why would quiet devotion need its own music? Because a lot of devotion is quiet. Sikh practice has its great public moments, the processions, the gatherings, the langar lines.

But it also lives in small repeated acts: reciting a bani in the morning, a whispered Waheguru, sweeping a floor. Gujri gives that side of faith a sound. It doesn't try to stir a crowd; it keeps company with one person.

The raga is named in the shabad's own heading, so in the tradition of singing the Granth in its ragas, the text chooses the music, not the singer's mood that day. A shabad headed Gujri is set to be sung in Gujri.
So the quiet is part of the instruction: the Guru set these words to be heard softly, and the music guards that.

how: Ragis sing shabads written in Gujri in Raga Gujri, since in Sikh kirtan the raga is set by the heading of the shabad; tradition places Gujri in the morning hours.

games.q: you're a ragi, and the shabad in front of you is headed Gujri. the crowd is big and you'd like something rousing. what do you sing it in?
o: Raga Gujri, as the heading says.
games.why: in Sikh kirtan the text chooses the raga. the quiet of Gujri is part of how the Guru set the words to be heard.

practice: Breathe a little more softly than usual, as if someone nearby were asleep, and think of one small thing you do faithfully that nobody notices: a call to a parent, feeding a pet on time, a glass of water for someone else.
Let it count, without making it bigger. If you pray, whisper Waheguru once, as quietly as you can and still hear it; if you don't, let the quiet itself be enough.
